analysis.problem_summary: Rotate an n x n 2D matrix 90 degrees clockwise in-place without allocating extra 2D matrix memory.
analysis.intuition: A 90-degree clockwise matrix rotation can be decomposed into two simpler linear matrix operations: transposing the matrix along its main diagonal (swapping matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i]), followed by flipping the matrix horizontally (reversing each row).
approach: Iterate over the upper triangle of the matrix (where j > i) and swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] to transpose the matrix.
Iterate through each row of the transposed matrix.
For each row, swap elements from the left half with elements from the right half (matrix[i][j] with matrix[i][n - 1 - j]) to reverse the row.
The matrix is now fully rotated 90 degrees clockwise in-place.
analysis.why_it_works: Transposition converts rows to columns such that top-to-bottom elements become left-to-right elements. Reversing each row then mirrors the values horizontally, which matches the exact mapping of a 90-degree clockwise rotation: cell (i, j) moves to (j, n - 1 - i).
analysis.key_takeaway: Decomposing complex matrix rotations into fundamental transformations like diagonal transposition and row reflection makes the code simple, readable, and easy to implement in-place.
analysis.time_explanation: Transposing touches each element above the main diagonal once (n*(n-1)/2 swaps). Reversing each row touches n/2 elements per row (n*(n/2) swaps). Overall operations are proportional to the total number of cells, giving O(n^2) time complexity for an n x n matrix.
analysis.space_explanation: The algorithm swaps elements in-place using a single primitive variable for temporary storage, requiring O(1) auxiliary space.

analysis.problem_summary: Rotate an n x n matrix 90 degrees clockwise directly in-place.
analysis.intuition: When rotating a square matrix by 90 degrees, elements move in 4-tuples. Top-left moves to top-right, top-right to bottom-right, bottom-right to bottom-left, and bottom-left to top-left. We can process the matrix layer by layer from the outermost boundary inward.
approach: Iterate through concentric square layers from outer ring i = 0 to inner ring i = n / 2.
For each element j along the top edge of the current layer, identify the four corresponding symmetric positions across the four edges.
Perform a cyclic shift of the 4 values in-place using temporary variables.
Repeat until all concentric layers are rotated.
analysis.why_it_works: Every cell in an n x n matrix belongs to a group of 4 cells that rotate into each other's positions. By directly swapping these 4 elements at once ring by ring, no cell is overwritten before its value is preserved.
analysis.key_takeaway: A layer-by-layer 4-way cyclic swap rotates the matrix in a single pass without needing a secondary global matrix transformation.
analysis.time_explanation: Each element in the matrix is part of a 4-element group, and each 4-element group is processed exactly once in O(1) time. Total operations scale directly with total matrix cells n^2, resulting in O(n^2) time.
analysis.space_explanation: The rotation is performed directly on the input array using a constant number of temporary scalar variables, taking O(1) extra space.
